topic.subject: science
topic.title: Electricity
topic.scope: charge, current, potential difference, Ohm's law, resistance and resistivity, series and parallel, heating effect, power

misconceptions.statement: Current is consumed by the bulb as it flows through the circuit.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the flow of electricity with the consumption of fuel like petrol or food.
misconceptions.fix: Current is a flow of charge that is conserved; the same amount of current enters and leaves a device.

probe.question: In a series circuit with two bulbs, is the current at point A (before the bulbs) greater than at point B (after the bulbs)?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the bulbs use up some of the current.

misconceptions.statement: Batteries are sources of constant current regardless of the circuit.
misconceptions.why: Students generalize from the idea that a battery 'contains' electricity and pushes it out.
misconceptions.fix: A battery provides a constant potential difference; the current depends on the resistance of the circuit.

probe.question: If you connect a wire directly across a battery, does the current remain the same as when a bulb is connected?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the battery always pushes the same amount of current.

misconceptions.statement: Voltage is a property of a single point in a circuit.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often label points as '12V' or '5V' without emphasizing that this is relative to ground.
misconceptions.fix: Potential difference is the work done to move charge between two distinct points.

probe.question: Can a point in a circuit have a voltage without being connected to anything else?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every point has its own fixed voltage.

misconceptions.statement: Resistance is a property of the current, not the conductor.
misconceptions.why: Students misinterpret Ohm's Law (V=IR) as R=V/I, thinking resistance changes when current changes.
misconceptions.fix: Resistance is an inherent property of the material and its dimensions, independent of the current flowing through it.

probe.question: If you double the voltage across a resistor, what happens to its resistance?
probe.wrong_answer: The resistance doubles because the current increases.

misconceptions.statement: Adding more resistors in parallel increases the total resistance of the circuit.
misconceptions.why: Students intuitively apply the additive logic of series circuits to parallel ones.
misconceptions.fix: Adding resistors in parallel provides more paths for current, which decreases the total resistance.

probe.question: If you add a second resistor in parallel to an existing one, what happens to the total resistance?
probe.wrong_answer: It increases because there is more resistance in the circuit.

misconceptions.statement: A device with a higher power rating always draws more current regardless of the voltage.
misconceptions.why: Students often ignore the relationship between power, voltage, and current, focusing only on the 'power' label.
misconceptions.fix: Power depends on both voltage and current (P=VI); a device's power rating is specific to its rated voltage.

probe.question: If two bulbs have different power ratings, does the one with higher power always have more current flowing through it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, higher power always means more current.
